newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage-backeds slip, prepay strategies key.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage-backeds slip, prepay strategies key.

text.p: U.S. mortgage-backeds took cues from U.S. Treasuries and trended down slightly Tuesday, with prepayment hedging strategies still dominant.
Treasury rates were slightly above triggers for home refinancings and early mortgage securities prepayments.

But with the when-issued 10-year Treasury note just seven basis points above a prepayment catalyst, "It's worrisome for people in premiums," said Art Frank, vice president of mortgage research at HSBC Markets Inc. Mortgage securities are prepaid at par, meaning losses for investors who hold high-coupon bonds, which now trade between 103 and 109.

Among key issues, Ginnie Mae 30-year 7-1/2 percent coupons were down 8/32 at 101-8/32 bid to yield 105 basis points over 10-year Treasuries. Comparable Fannie Maes were down 7/32 at 101-5/32 and Freddie Macs were down 5/32 at 101-10/32.
So-called pool factor tapes of raw data used to measure prepayments were released by the Federal National Mortgage Association and the Government National Mortgage Association.

Michael Youngblood, head of mortgage research at Chase Securities Inc, said "detailed reports will probably not reach most investors for another day or two. It takes another day or two to review" and respond to the data."
In addition to down-in-coupon trades, another prepayment bet has been to unwind interest-only securities (IOs) holdings and instead buy principal-only securities (POs).
Traders said they weren't as worried about IOs as in 1993, when the 10-year yielded as low as 5.17 percent.

"Everyone who owned IOs then got slaughtered," said Frank. Still, IOs "have cheapened up considerably with this (Treasuries) rally" and taking the conservative side of that trade -- buying POs -- has gotten more costly, he said.
Prepayments hurt IOs, which pay only interest, by drying up cash streams to investors earlier than expected. Mortgage payments are predominantly interest in the initial years.

Frank advised underweighting mortgages, if strongly bullish about a continued bond rally. Otherwise, he suggested buying intermediate-type securities derived from discount collateral. ((-- Lynn Adler, 212-859-1677, & Alexsandrs Rozens,
